theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: The Permanent Secretary asks Marcia Campbell, a director in a ministry, to 'bring in consultants to fix the records unit'. What should Marcia do first?
options: Define the problem and the result the ministry needs
Ask three well-known firms to send their day rates
Draft the consultancy contract from an old template
Set up a steering committee to choose the firm

questions.stem: Which situation best justifies hiring a consultant rather than using the agency's own staff?
options: The work is routine and staff have done it every year
The agency needs a specialist skill for a short, set period
The manager wants an outsider to carry the blame for a decision
The budget has money left near the end of the financial year

questions.stem: A parish council plans to pay a consultant to process its payroll every month for three years. What is the main concern with this plan?
options: Consultants may never see any payroll data at all
Three years is too short a period for any consultancy contract to run
It is ongoing core work, better suited to a post or service contract
Payroll work in councils must be done by the Auditor General's own staff

questions.stem: Before going to market for a consultant, why should a public body confirm that money is approved in its budget for the work?
options: So that the consultant can be paid in advance
So that the price can be kept secret from the firms
So that no written contract will be needed later
So that it does not commit public money it cannot pay

questions.stem: An agency estimates a consultancy at 40 days for one consultant at J$45,000 a day, before GCT. What is the fee estimate?
What is the main purpose of the terms of reference (TOR) for a consultancy?
options: To set out the background, scope, outputs and timing of the work
To record the consultant's personal details and bank account
To list the reasons why staff could not do the work themselves
To show the final report the client hopes the consultant will write

questions.stem: A draft TOR says the consultant will 'review and improve customer service'. What is the main weakness?
options: It is too short to be read by the bidding firms
It names customer service, which is a private-sector idea
It does not state the outputs, standards or deadlines
It should have been written by the consultant instead

questions.stem: Which item is a deliverable rather than an activity in a consultancy TOR?
options: Interviewing staff in the three regional offices
Visiting the Spanish Town and May Pen branches
Reviewing the agency's existing complaint files
A final report with costed recommendations

questions.stem: Why should the TOR state which staff, data and office space the client will provide to the consultant?
options: So that the consultant can charge for using them
So that bidders can price the work and plan it accurately
So that staff do not need to meet the consultant at all
So that the client can avoid signing a contract

questions.stem: What do the procurement rules for public bodies mainly aim to achieve when a consultant is selected?
options: The quickest possible award, whatever the method used
The choice of the firm best known to the minister
Fair competition, transparency and value for money
The lowest price, whatever the quality offered

questions.stem: Damion Reid wants to hire, without competition, a consultant he worked with before, because 'she is good'. What is the correct position?
options: Direct selection is used only where the rules allow it and the reason is recorded
Direct selection is always acceptable when the manager knows and trusts the consultant
Direct selection is never allowed for any public consultancy
Direct selection is fine if the fee is split into smaller contracts

questions.stem: An agency publishes a notice asking firms to show their interest and experience before it sends out the full request for proposals. What is this stage called?
options: A purchase order for the consultancy work
A request for expressions of interest
A notice of award to the chosen firm
A letter of award

questions.stem: Twelve firms respond to an agency's notice. How should the shortlist be drawn up?
options: By choosing the firms whose staff the panel knows best
By keeping only firms based in Kingston for easy meetings
By picking the first five responses that arrived
By scoring each firm against criteria published in the notice

questions.stem: What should a request for proposals (RFP) tell the shortlisted firms about evaluation?
options: The criteria, their weights and how price will be scored
Nothing, so that firms cannot shape their proposals to it
Only the name of the panel chair and the closing date
The budget, so firms can bid exactly that amount

questions.stem: One shortlisted firm emails a question about the scope. What should the agency do with the question and its answer?
options: Answer that firm only, as it asked first
Ignore it, because no questions are allowed once the RFP has gone out
Send the answer to all shortlisted firms, without naming who asked
Answer by phone so that there is no written record

questions.stem: A proposal arrives two hours after the published closing time. What normally happens?
options: It is opened first, as a sign of good faith
It is accepted if the firm gives a good excuse
It is accepted if its price is the lowest
It is rejected and returned or recorded unopened

questions.stem: Why do many public bodies score the technical proposals before opening the price proposals?
options: So that the panel can finish the work faster
So that quality is judged without being swayed by price
So that the cheapest firm is always chosen at the end
So that firms can change their prices after scoring

questions.stem: The RFP sets a minimum technical score of 70 points. Firm C scores 65 points but offers by far the lowest price. What should happen?
options: Firm C wins because price matters most for public money
Firm C is asked to rewrite its technical proposal
Firm C is not considered further, whatever its price
Firm C's score is raised to 70 to keep it in the race

questions.stem: The financial score is the lowest price divided by the firm's price, times 100. The lowest price is J$4,800,000 and Firm A bid J$6,000,000. What is Firm A's financial score?
Technical counts 80% and price 20%. Firm A: technical 85, financial 80. Firm B: technical 78, financial 100. Which firm ranks first, and why?
options: Firm B, with 82.4 against 84 for Firm A
Firm B, because its price is the lowest
Firm A, with 84 against 82.4 for Firm B
Firm A, because its technical score is the highest

questions.stem: A member of the evaluation panel finds that her brother-in-law is a partner in one bidding firm. What should she do?
options: Score that firm lower to show she is fair
Keep quiet, as she has not worked with him
Score only the price proposals, not the technical ones
Declare the interest and step off the panel

questions.stem: A firm that wrote the TOR for an agency now wants to bid to do the work. What is the main risk?
options: It may have shaped the TOR to suit itself, an unfair advantage
It will not understand the work well enough to carry it out properly
It will be too busy with other clients to start the work on time
It may charge too little and make a loss

questions.stem: During evaluation, a bidder invites the panel chair to lunch 'to explain our approach'. What should the chair do?
options: Accept, as long as the whole panel goes too
Decline and keep all contact through the formal channel
Accept, but pay for her own meal
Decline only if the lunch costs more than J$5,000

questions.stem: After selection, what is a proper subject for contract negotiation with the top-ranked firm?
options: Replacing its proposed team with less qualified staff
Dropping the main deliverables to lower the price
Reducing the technical score of the second firm
Work plan details, timing and the client's inputs

questions.stem: Shanice Brown's agency has chosen a firm. An unsuccessful bidder asks why it lost. What is the best response?
options: Refuse, as all evaluation details must always be kept secret
Send it copies of the other firms' full proposals and prices
Offer a debriefing on its own proposal's strengths and gaps
Tell it only that the panel preferred the winning firm's staff

questions.stem: Which contract type best suits a consultancy with clear, fixed outputs that can be priced in advance?
options: A lump-sum contract paid against deliverables
A time-based contract with no cap on days
A verbal agreement confirmed by email later
A retainer paid monthly whatever is produced

questions.stem: A consultant will design a new training manual for a public agency. Which contract clause matters most for the agency's later use of it?
options: The clause setting the consultant's office hours and days of work
The clause on who owns the intellectual property in the work
The clause on the colour of the report cover
The clause on parking at the agency's offices

questions.stem: A consultant will see citizens' personal records during the work. What should the contract include?
options: A promise that the records will be shared only with the press
Permission for the consultant to keep copies of the records for later projects
A rule that staff must not speak to the consultant
Confidentiality and data protection duties, and return of the data

questions.stem: A J$5,000,000 contract pays 20% on the inception report, 30% on the draft report and 50% on the final report. After the draft is accepted, how much has been paid?
Why should consultancy payments be linked to accepted deliverables rather than paid as a large advance?
options: Because consultants usually prefer to wait until the end for their money
Because it lowers the GCT payable on the contract
Because advances are banned in every contract
Because the client pays only for work that meets the agreed standard

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the inception report early in a consultancy?
options: To confirm the consultant's understanding, method and work plan
To give the consultant's final findings and recommendations to the board
To record the reasons the losing firms did not win
To pay the consultant's travel costs in advance

questions.stem: At the inception meeting, the consultant's team leader is not the person named in the proposal. What should the contract manager do?
options: Accept the change, as all consultants are much the same
Require an equal or better replacement, approved in writing
End the contract at once without discussion
Ask the original team leader to attend just the meetings

questions.stem: Who in the client body should normally manage the consultant from day to day?
options: The Minister, who has political responsibility
Any staff member the consultant chooses to ask
A named contract manager with clear authority
The procurement committee that chose the firm

questions.stem: Halfway through a six-month contract, the consultant has not sent the agreed fortnightly progress reports. What should the contract manager do first?
options: Raise it with the consultant in writing and agree how to fix it
Stop all payments to the consultant for the rest of the contract
Ask staff to do the consultant's work instead
Wait for the final report and judge it then

questions.stem: A steering committee oversees a large consultancy at an agency. What is its main role?
options: To write the consultant's reports for him
To give direction, resolve issues and accept key outputs
To meet only after the contract has ended
To approve the consultant's daily timesheets

questions.stem: Staff in a Montego Bay office refuse to give data to the consultant because they fear job cuts. What should the manager do?
options: Tell the consultant to finish the work without that office's data
Order staff to comply and give no reason
Ask the consultant to guess the missing figures
Explain the purpose of the work and agree how data will be used

questions.stem: The director wants the consultant to add a review of a second unit that is not in the TOR. What should happen?
options: The consultant simply adds it and bills for the time
The director tells the consultant verbally to fit it into the present work
A written variation is agreed and approved before the extra work starts
The extra work is done and the contract is changed afterwards

questions.stem: A J$4,000,000 contract is varied to add 10 days at J$50,000 a day. By what percentage does the contract value rise?
Small requests keep being added to a consultancy without any change to the contract. What is this problem usually called?
options: Scope creep
Value for money
Due diligence
Knowledge transfer

questions.stem: The draft report is well written but does not answer two of the five questions in the TOR. What should the contract manager do?
options: Accept it, since most of the work is done and the rest can follow
Rewrite the missing parts herself
Pay in full and ask for the rest as a favour
Return it with written comments against the TOR before accepting

questions.stem: How can an agency best make sure its own staff can keep a new system running after the consultant leaves?
options: Rely on the consultant's phone number to sort out any later problems
Build training, manuals and staff shadowing into the contract
Ask the consultant to keep the system's passwords
Hire the same consultant again each year

questions.stem: What is the main risk of an agency relying on the same consultant for many years?
options: The consultant will charge less over time
The staff will learn too much from the consultant
The agency becomes dependent and loses its own skills
The consultant will stop sending invoices

questions.stem: A consultant and the agency disagree on whether a deliverable meets the TOR. What should be tried first?
options: Go straight to court
Post the dispute on social media
Stop speaking to the consultant
Discuss and use the contract's dispute steps

questions.stem: At the end of a consultancy, which question is most useful for judging its success?
options: Did the outputs meet the TOR, on time and within budget, and are they being used?
Did the consultant attend every staff meeting and social event during the contract?
Was the final report longer than the reports the agency usually receives?
Did the consultant agree with every view the director held at the start?

questions.stem: Why must the full file of a public consultancy (TOR, evaluation, contract, reports and payments) be kept?
options: So that the consultant can reuse the reports for other paying clients
So that the agency can show auditors how public money was spent
So that staff can avoid writing reports of their own
So that the price can be kept secret from the auditors

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What three-word term names the document that sets out the background, scope, outputs and timing of a consultancy?
What is the notice called that asks firms to show their interest and experience, so that a shortlist can be drawn up? (Three words, or the letters.)
What is the document called that invites shortlisted firms to send technical and price proposals? (Three words, or the letters.)
What is the early report called in which the consultant confirms the method and work plan?
A consultant will work 25 days at J$40,000 a day. What is the fee, before GCT, in J$?
The lowest price is J$3,000,000. Firm D bid J$4,000,000. Using lowest price ÷ firm's price × 100, what is Firm D's financial score?
What two-word term describes the gradual, uncontrolled growth of the work beyond what the contract covers?
What is the formal written change to a consultancy contract's scope, time or price usually called? (One word.)
What three-word term names a situation in which a panel member's private interest could affect their judgement?
What two-word term names the passing of a consultant's skills and know-how to the client's own staff?
What two-word term names a contract in which the consultant is paid one agreed total for set outputs, whatever days are worked?
What one-word term names a specific output, such as a report or a manual, that the consultant must hand over?
A J$6,000,000 contract pays 25% when the inception report is accepted. How much is that payment, in J$?
What two-word title is usually given to the client officer named to oversee the consultant from day to day?
What three-word phrase names the aim of getting the best mix of quality, cost and results from public spending?

essays.stem: Your agency must redesign its licence application process. Evaluate whether to use a consultant or the agency's own staff, and make a justified recommendation.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first define the work: map the present process, find delays, design a new process and help staff adopt it. Using our own staff costs less in fees, keeps knowledge in the agency and builds ownership, but our process team is small, busy with daily work and has no one trained in process redesign, so the work could take a year or more and may repeat old habits. A consultant brings specialist method, an outside view and dedicated time, and can finish in about four months, but costs fees, needs careful management and leaves with the know-how unless we plan for transfer. There is also a risk that staff resist outside advice. On balance I recommend a consultant for the design work, if the budget allows, with two of our officers working beside them full time and a contract that requires training, a procedures manual and a handover. This gives speed and skill while building our own capacity and ownership.
markingPoints: Defines the work and the skills, time and capacity it needs
Weighs the benefits and drawbacks of in-house staff (cost, ownership, capacity, skill)
Weighs the benefits and drawbacks of a consultant (skill, speed, cost, dependency, resistance)
Makes a clear recommendation linked to budget and value for money
Builds in knowledge transfer or staff involvement so the agency keeps the skills

essays.stem: Describe what you would include in the terms of reference for a consultant to review customer service at a parish council, and explain why each part matters.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start with background: the council's services, the number of customers and the problems seen, such as long queues and complaints, so bidders understand the context. Next the objectives: what the council wants to achieve, for example shorter waiting times and fewer repeat complaints. The scope sets what is in and out, such as the front counter and phone line but not the market or the pound, which stops scope creep. The activities and method expected, such as surveys and staff interviews, help bidders plan. The deliverables, with standards and dates (inception report, survey findings, draft and final report with costed recommendations) are what we pay for. I would state the client's inputs (data, a contact officer, office space), the team and skills required, the reporting lines and steering arrangements, the timescale, and how the proposals will be evaluated. A clear TOR lets firms price fairly, makes evaluation objective and gives the contract manager a standard to judge the work against.
markingPoints: Background and objectives that explain the need
Clear scope stating what is included and excluded
Deliverables with standards and deadlines, and the timescale
Client inputs, required skills, reporting lines and evaluation basis
Explains why a clear TOR matters (fair pricing, objective evaluation, managing the contract)

essays.stem: An RFP weights technical quality at 80% and price at 20%, with a 70-point technical minimum. Firm A scores 85 technical and bids J$6,000,000; Firm B scores 78 and bids J$4,800,000; Firm C scores 65 and bids J$3,900,000. The financial score is lowest valid price ÷ firm's price × 100. Work out the result and explain it.
essays.modelAnswer: Firm C scored 65 technical points, below the 70-point minimum, so it is not considered further and its price is not used. The lowest valid price is therefore Firm B's J$4,800,000. Firm B's financial score is 4,800,000 ÷ 4,800,000 × 100 = 100. Firm A's is 4,800,000 ÷ 6,000,000 × 100 = 80. The combined scores are: Firm A, 85 × 0.8 = 68 plus 80 × 0.2 = 16, giving 84; Firm B, 78 × 0.8 = 62.4 plus 100 × 0.2 = 20, giving 82.4. Firm A ranks first with 84 against 82.4, although it costs J$1,200,000 more. This is the purpose of a quality- and cost-based method: for advice that shapes a public service, a stronger proposal can be better value than a cheaper one. The panel should record each score and the reasons, check the sums, confirm no member had a conflict of interest, and then invite Firm A to negotiate, keeping Firm B as the reserve.
markingPoints: Excludes Firm C for failing the technical minimum, so its price is not used
Financial scores correct: Firm B 100, Firm A 80
Combined scores correct: Firm A 84, Firm B 82.4, so Firm A ranks first
Explains why the higher-priced firm can be better value
Records the scores and reasons and moves to negotiation with a reserve

essays.stem: Describe the steps a public body should follow to select a consultant fairly, from the approved need to the signed contract.
essays.modelAnswer: Once the need and the budget are approved, the body writes the terms of reference and a cost estimate, and chooses the selection method the procurement rules set for the type and value of the work. It usually publishes a request for expressions of interest, then scores the responses against published criteria to draw up a shortlist. The shortlisted firms receive a request for proposals giving the TOR, the evaluation criteria and weights, the closing date and how to submit. Questions are answered in writing to all firms. Proposals are opened at the stated time, with late ones refused. An evaluation panel, whose members have declared any conflicts of interest, scores the technical proposals first and then the prices, and writes an evaluation report. After approval, the body negotiates details with the top firm, issues the award, tells the unsuccessful firms and offers them a debriefing, and signs the contract. Every step is recorded so that it can be audited.
markingPoints: Approved need and budget, TOR and cost estimate, and the method the rules require
Expressions of interest and shortlisting against published criteria
RFP with criteria and weights; questions answered to all; late bids refused
Panel with conflict declarations scores technical then price, with an evaluation report and approval
Negotiation, award, notifying and debriefing others, contract signed, records kept

essays.stem: Explain the main clauses a public agency should make sure are in a consultancy contract, and why each protects the agency.
essays.modelAnswer: The contract should attach the TOR and the accepted proposal, so the scope and deliverables are binding. It should name the key staff and say they may be changed only with written approval of an equal replacement, which protects the quality the agency paid for. A payment schedule linked to accepted deliverables means public money is paid only for work that meets the standard. A clause on intellectual property should give the agency ownership or full rights to use the reports, tools and data, so it can use and adapt them later. Confidentiality and data protection duties protect citizens' information and require its return or safe deletion. A variation clause sets how changes are agreed in writing. There should be clauses on reporting, the contract manager's role, termination for poor performance, and dispute steps such as negotiation and mediation. Together these turn the agreement into something the agency can manage and enforce.
markingPoints: Scope: TOR and proposal attached, deliverables binding
Key staff named, with changes only by approval
Payments linked to accepted deliverables
Intellectual property, confidentiality and data protection
Variation, termination and dispute clauses, each linked to how it protects the agency

essays.stem: You are the contract manager for a six-month consultancy at a ministry. Plan how you will manage the consultant's performance from inception to final report.
essays.modelAnswer: At the inception meeting I would confirm the TOR, the work plan, the team, the client inputs and how we will communicate, and agree a reporting routine, such as a short progress report every two weeks. I would set up a simple tracker of each deliverable, its due date, its status and its payment. I would arrange the data, office space and staff access we promised, so we do not cause delays ourselves. I would hold fortnightly check-ins and a monthly steering committee meeting to give direction and settle issues. I would review each draft against the TOR, give written comments within agreed times, and approve payment only when a deliverable is accepted. If problems arise, such as missed reports or a weaker team member, I would raise them early in writing and agree corrective action, and use variations only for genuine changes in scope. At the end I would write a performance evaluation of the consultant and file all records.
markingPoints: Inception meeting confirming the work plan, team and reporting routine
Provides the client's inputs on time and tracks deliverables and payments
Regular check-ins and steering committee oversight
Reviews outputs against the TOR and pays only on acceptance
Deals with problems early and in writing, and evaluates the consultant at the end

essays.stem: Two months into a consultancy, the consultant's draft is late and of poor quality, and the named team leader has hardly appeared. Evaluate your options and recommend what to do.
essays.modelAnswer: My options are to accept the delay and wait, to raise the problems formally and agree a recovery plan, to hold back payment, or to end the contract. Waiting risks the whole project and wastes money. Ending the contract at once may be within our rights, but it loses two months, means a new procurement and may lead to a dispute if we have not given notice under the contract. I would first check the facts: the TOR, the work plan, the contract terms on key staff and deliverables, and whether we provided all our own inputs. Then I would write to the firm setting out the problems, meet its director, and require the named team leader to take part or be replaced by an approved person of equal standing, with a revised timetable. No payment would be made until the draft meets the TOR. If the plan fails, I would follow the termination steps in the contract with advice from procurement and legal staff. I recommend the formal recovery plan first.
markingPoints: Identifies the options: wait, recovery plan, withhold payment, terminate
Checks the contract terms and the client's own part before acting
Raises the problems formally in writing with a meeting and revised timetable
Enforces the key staff clause and withholds payment until work meets the TOR
Recommends a clear course, with termination by the contract's steps as a last resort

essays.stem: Prepare and explain a cost estimate for a consultancy that needs a team leader for 30 days at J$60,000 a day, two analysts for 40 days each at J$35,000 a day, and J$400,000 of expenses. Say how GCT and contingency should be treated.
essays.modelAnswer: The team leader costs 30 × J$60,000 = J$1,800,000. Each analyst costs 40 × J$35,000 = J$1,400,000, so the two cost J$2,800,000. Fees total J$1,800,000 + J$2,800,000 = J$4,600,000. Adding J$400,000 of expenses for travel, venues and printing gives J$5,000,000 before GCT. I would then add GCT at the current rate if the consultant is registered for it, because the agency pays the tax-inclusive amount and the budget must cover it. I would show a separate small contingency for likely changes, kept under the director's control and not told to bidders. The estimate is used to confirm that the budget can cover the work before procurement starts, to choose the procurement method that suits the value, and to judge whether bids are reasonable. I would note my assumptions, such as day rates from recent similar contracts, so that reviewers can check them.
markingPoints: Team leader J$1,800,000 and analysts J$2,800,000 correct
Fees J$4,600,000 and total J$5,000,000 before GCT correct
GCT added at the current rate, without stating a figure
Contingency shown separately and controlled
Explains the uses of the estimate and records assumptions

essays.stem: Explain the integrity risks in obtaining consultancy services for a public body, and how a manager should guard against each one.
essays.modelAnswer: One risk is favouritism: steering work to a friend, relative or former colleague. The manager guards against it by competing the work as the procurement rules require, recording any direct selection with its reason, and making all panel members declare conflicts of interest and step aside where needed. A second risk is a firm writing a TOR that suits itself and then bidding, which is avoided by keeping TOR writers out of the competition. A third is gifts or hospitality from bidders, which staff should refuse during the process and report, under the code of conduct. A fourth is splitting a contract to avoid the method required for its value. A fifth is leaking information, such as one bidder's price, to another. All contact with bidders should go through one formal channel, with answers shared with every firm. Finally, paying for work not done is prevented by paying only on accepted deliverables. A full, auditable file shows that public money was used properly.
markingPoints: Favouritism and conflict of interest, with declarations and competition
Unfair advantage from writing the TOR, and contract splitting
Gifts and hospitality refused and reported under the code of conduct
Confidential bid information protected; one formal channel of contact
Payment only on accepted work and a full, auditable file

essays.stem: A consultancy at your agency has ended. Describe how you would evaluate it and justify why the evaluation matters.
essays.modelAnswer: I would compare what was delivered with the TOR: were all deliverables produced, to the agreed standard, on time and within the contract price, including any approved variations? I would ask the steering committee and the staff who worked with the consultant about the quality of the advice, the team's skills and conduct, and how well knowledge was passed on. I would check whether the recommendations are being used, for example whether the new process has cut waiting times as planned, which may mean a follow-up review after six months. I would also review our own part: was the TOR clear, did we provide data on time, and did we manage the contract well? The findings go into a short performance report on the consultant, kept on file for future selections, and a lessons-learned note for the agency. This matters because it shows whether public money gave value, improves future TORs and contracts, and gives fair, recorded evidence for choosing consultants later.
markingPoints: Compares deliverables, quality, time and cost with the TOR and contract
Gathers views from the steering committee and staff, including knowledge transfer
Checks whether the recommendations are being used and the results achieved
Reviews the agency's own role and records a performance report and lessons learned
Justifies the evaluation (value for money, accountability, better future selections)

practical1.title: Write the terms of reference and evaluation plan for a consultancy
practical1.brief: Your group is a project team in a public agency. The assessor gives you a scenario (for example, a parish council that wants outside help to cut waiting times at its front counter, or an agency that needs a review of its records system). Prepare the documents needed to go to market for a consultant. Give each member a named role: team lead (keeps the plan and checks consistency), TOR writer for background, objectives and scope, TOR writer for deliverables and timing, cost estimator (prepares a day-rate estimate before GCT, with GCT 'at the current rate' and a contingency line), and in a group of five an evaluation planner (criteria, weights, minimum technical score and the price formula). Together produce: (1) a TOR of 2 to 3 pages; (2) a cost estimate with the sums shown; (3) an evaluation sheet with criteria and weights; and (4) a one-page note to the director justifying why a consultant is needed rather than staff. Each member presents their part to the assessor for 3 minutes. Photograph each document and hand in once for the group.
materials: Computer with word processor and spreadsheet, and a printer, or paper and pens
Sample TOR headings sheet and blank evaluation sheet
photos: The planning flipchart showing each member's name, role and tasks
The completed TOR, with the scope and the deliverables table visible
The cost estimate with every sum shown
The evaluation sheet with criteria, weights, minimum score and price formula
The one-page justification note and a member presenting to the assessor
checklist: Carried out a named role and produced their own part of the evidence
TOR states background, objectives, scope (in and out), deliverables, deadlines and client inputs
Cost estimate is correct, with days, rates, expenses, contingency and GCT at the current rate
Evaluation criteria and weights are clear, fair and linked to the TOR
Justification note explains why a consultant is needed and how skills will pass to staff
Presented their part clearly and answered the assessor's questions
Checked another member's work for consistency with the TOR
safety: Use made-up names and figures: no real agency's confidential data
Store drafts in the Centre's shared folder only and delete copies from personal devices
Respect each member's ideas and share the workload fairly
Take a short screen break each hour when working at a computer

practical2.title: Manage a failing consultancy: progress review meeting and recovery plan
practical2.brief: Your group manages a consultancy for a ministry. The assessor gives you a pack: the TOR, the contract's key clauses, the payment schedule and a late, weak draft report from the consultant. Give each member a named role: contract manager (leads the meeting), steering committee chair, finance officer (works out payments made and due), records officer (takes minutes and keeps the action log), and in a group of five a second member who reviews the draft against the TOR. One member, or the assessor, plays the consultant's director. First, review the draft against the TOR and list the gaps in writing. Next, hold a 25-minute progress review meeting with the consultant to agree a recovery plan: revised dates, the named team leader's role and what will be paid and when. Then write a one-page recovery plan and a letter to the consultant confirming what was agreed. Photograph each stage.
materials: Assessor's pack: TOR, key contract clauses, payment schedule, draft report
Computer with word processor, or paper and pens
Gap-review sheet, minutes template and action log
photos: The gap review of the draft against each TOR item
The finance officer's working of payments made and payments due
The progress review meeting in progress, with roles shown on name cards
The minutes and action log, with owners and dates
The recovery plan and the letter to the consultant
checklist: Carried out a named role and contributed to the written evidence
Gap review compares the draft with each TOR item accurately
Payment working is correct and links payment to accepted deliverables only
In the meeting, raised problems firmly and politely, using the contract terms
Recovery plan sets revised dates, the key staff position and the next steps if it fails
Letter confirms the agreement clearly and professionally
Minutes record decisions and actions neutrally
safety: Keep the role play respectful: challenge the work, not the person
Use only made-up names; do not refer to any real firm or officer
Treat the pack as confidential and collect all copies at the end
Share tasks fairly so that no member carries the whole load
